title: Adjective endings
theoryMd:
Adjective endings have a reputation as the hardest part of German grammar. They are not conceptually hard — there is one idea and three small tables — but they do require the case system to be automatic first. If you are still hesitating over *den* vs *dem*, work on that before this.

## The one idea

An adjective only takes an ending when it stands **in front of a noun**. After *sein*, *werden* or *bleiben* it stays bare:

- *Das Haus ist **groß**.* — no ending
- *Das **große** Haus* — ending

And the ending depends on a single question: **has the case and gender already been shown by the article?** German marks each noun phrase for case and gender exactly once. If the article does it, the adjective can relax. If the article is missing or vague, the adjective has to do the job itself.

That gives three patterns.

## 1. Weak endings — after *der/die/das*

When a definite article precedes, all the information is already visible, so the adjective takes an almost uniform ending: **-e** or **-en**. Only five slots get *-e*, and everything else is *-en*.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **nom** | der gut**e** | die gut**e** | das gut**e** | die gut**en** |
| **acc** | den gut**en** | die gut**e** | das gut**e** | die gut**en** |
| **dat** | dem gut**en** | der gut**en** | dem gut**en** | den gut**en** |

The shape is easy to remember visually: the *-e* forms sit in the **top-left corner** (nominative singular, plus feminine and neuter accusative). Everything below and to the right is *-en*.

The same pattern follows *dieser, jener, jeder, welcher, alle*.

## 2. Mixed endings — after *ein/kein/mein*

The indefinite article has a problem: *ein* is ambiguous. *Ein guter Wein* and *ein gutes Bier* both start with the same *ein*, so the article cannot tell you the gender. In exactly those three ambiguous slots, the adjective steps in and takes the **strong** ending instead.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **nom** | ein gut**er** | eine gut**e** | ein gut**es** | keine gut**en** |
| **acc** | einen gut**en** | eine gut**e** | ein gut**es** | keine gut**en** |
| **dat** | einem gut**en** | einer gut**en** | einem gut**en** | keinen gut**en** |

Compare with the weak table: it is **identical except for three cells** — masculine nominative (*-er*) and neuter nominative/accusative (*-es*). Those are precisely the places where *ein* has no ending of its own.

> If you learn only one thing here, learn those three: *ein gut**er** Mann*, *ein gut**es** Kind* (twice). Everything else after *ein-* is *-e* or *-en*, exactly as after *der*.

## 3. Strong endings — no article at all

With no article, nothing has marked the case, so the adjective takes over the article's own endings almost exactly:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **nom** | gut**er** Wein | gut**e** Milch | gut**es** Bier | gut**e** Weine |
| **acc** | gut**en** Wein | gut**e** Milch | gut**es** Bier | gut**e** Weine |
| **dat** | gut**em** Wein | gut**er** Milch | gut**em** Bier | gut**en** Weinen |

Notice these are essentially the endings of *der/die/das* itself: *der → -er*, *das → -es*, *dem → -em*, *die → -e*. If you know the article forms, you already know this table.

This pattern shows up more than beginners expect: with uncountable nouns (*Ich trinke **kaltes** Wasser*), with plurals lacking an article (*Sie hat **nette** Freunde*), after numbers (*drei **große** Häuser*), and after *viele, wenige, einige, mehrere, etwas, nichts*.

## A working procedure

When you build a phrase, run these three questions in order:

1. **Is there an article?** No → strong table (adjective takes the article's ending).
2. **Is it *der/die/das*?** Yes → weak table (*-e* in the top-left corner, otherwise *-en*).
3. **Is it *ein/kein/mein*?** Then it is the weak table **except** the three ambiguous slots: *-er* masculine nominative, *-es* neuter nominative and accusative.

With practice this collapses into a feel. Two shortcuts speed it up enormously:

- **Everything plural that follows any article word is *-en*.** *die guten, meine guten, keinen guten* — no exceptions.
- **Everything dative is *-en***, except feminine dative after no article (*guter Milch*) and the strong masculine/neuter *-em*.

## Several adjectives, and a spelling trap

When adjectives stack, they all take the same ending: *ein gut**er**, alt**er**, deutsch**er** Wein.*

Watch three irregular stems:

- **hoch** loses its *-c-*: *ein **hoher** Berg* (not *hocher*)
- **teuer** and **dunkel** drop the *-e-*: *ein **teurer** Wein*, *ein **dunkler** Raum*
- adjectives from city names add *-er* and never change: *der **Berliner** Bär*, *in der **Berliner** Straße*

payload.explanation: After sein/werden/bleiben the adjective stands alone and takes NO ending.
Weak ending after the definite article, masculine nominative: der gute Wein.
'ein' shows no gender here, so the adjective takes the strong ending: ein guter Wein.
Neuter nominative after 'ein' is one of the three ambiguous slots: ein gutes Bier.
Masculine accusative after the definite article is weak -en: den guten Wein.

payload.prompt: Ich trinke gut___ Wein. (no article, accusative)
payload.explanation: No article → strong ending, mirroring 'den': guten Wein.

payload.prompt: Ich trinke kalt___ Wasser. (no article, neuter accusative)
payload.explanation: Strong neuter accusative mirrors 'das': kaltes Wasser.
Dative after a definite article is always -en: mit dem neuen Auto.

payload.prompt: Sie hat nett___ Freunde. (plural, no article)
payload.explanation: Strong plural nominative/accusative mirrors 'die': nette Freunde.
Every plural following an article word takes -en, with no exceptions.
'hoch' drops its -c- before an ending: hoher, hohe, hohen.
'teuer' drops the -e- of the stem before an ending: teurer, teure, teuren.
